assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients discrete-choice demand estimation with endogenous prices and equilibrium supply, together with dynamic oligopoly models, changed how demand, market power, mergers and welfare are measured. It is now the standard toolkit in industrial organisation, antitrust and trade, with applications well beyond the field. The methodological contribution is transformative and the empirical reach is wide.
assessment.attribution: The core demand-estimation framework is credited to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995), and Berry's inversion is central. Pakes adds the dynamic-games and production-function strands. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are also important to the broader agenda, but a three-person cap forces choices. Bresnahan, who pioneered the New Empirical IO, is the most serious omission.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from the 1980s to the 1990s and has been confirmed over three decades in practice, including regulatory use. The timing is ripe, and the field has not yet been recognised by the prize in this form.
uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan should displace Levinsohn.
Whether the committee prefers a narrower methods framing or a broader IO framing.
I work in a neighbouring field and have tried to apply common criteria and not a field preference.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work built a unified, empirically tested political economics. It connects electoral rules, constitutions, accountability and state capacity to fiscal policy and development outcomes. It has shaped a large research program and informs institutional design.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are jointly credited with the constitutional and electoral-rule program and the 2000 and 2003 books. Besley contributed accountability, state-capacity and fiscal work, often with Persson. The three-person grouping is coherent and the credit is reasonably well delineated.
assessment.maturity: The work is over 25 years old and has been widely validated and extended. A prize would follow the 2024 institutions prize, so there is some thematic proximity to weigh.
uncertainties: Thematic overlap with the 2024 institutions laureates.
The share of credit within the broader political-economy field, including Alesina and others.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their political-economy model of trade protection ('Protection for Sale') and their joint endogenous-growth-and-trade framework are foundational. Together they link trade theory, interest-group politics and innovation. They have been influential in both theory and empirical trade-policy research.
assessment.attribution: The credit is cleanly shared between the two as a long-standing pair, and the pairing is natural. Helpman also appears under firm heterogeneity (B050), so a prize here would partly cover his other contributions.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from the 1990s and has been confirmed by decades of use and testing. There is no timing concern.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2008 trade prize to Krugman.
Whether the committee values the political-economy strand over the growth-and-trade strand.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The sufficient-statistics approach, the elasticity of taxable income and evidence-based optimal taxation connect theory directly to measurable behaviour and policy. The field is influential across public economics, with strong policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod is the senior figure on taxable-income and avoidance behaviour. Saez developed the empirical optimal-tax and top-income agenda, and Chetty developed sufficient statistics. Stantcheva is excluded because her career is still early. Saez and Chetty also appear in other candidacies, which raises the risk of fragmented credit.
assessment.maturity: The work is 15 to 25 years old. Parts are well confirmed, but some of the ETI literature remains debated and the Chetty portfolio is still evolving.
uncertainties: Whether Feldstein's foundational ETI role (he is deceased) distorts how credit is assigned.
Overlap with the inequality and mobility candidacies (B030, B017).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Staggered pricing and contracts, the Taylor rule and the microfounded New Keynesian framework underpin modern central-bank practice. The framework is central to monetary-policy analysis. I find the nominal-rigidity microfoundations especially notable, as price setting is a topic I know well.
assessment.attribution: The credit is highly diffuse across Calvo (pricing), Taylor (contracts and the rule), Woodford (synthesis), Gali, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum, Smets and others. Any three-person selection is contestable, and this is the main weakness of the candidacy.
assessment.maturity: The work is 30 to 40 years old and has long been confirmed in policy use. Some empirical aspects of the framework are debated, especially after the 2008 crisis and the 2021 to 2022 inflation.
uncertainties: Genuinely diffuse attribution.
Whether a three-person cap can properly represent the field.
Possible tension with my own empirical work, which finds mixed evidence on menu costs and asymmetric adjustment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints that amplify and propagate shocks (Kiyotaki–Moore) and the financial accelerator became core to macro-finance and to understanding crisis dynamics. The influence on policy analysis is clear, especially after 2008.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are clearly the pair for credit cycles. Gertler's inclusion rests on the financial accelerator with Bernanke and Gilchrist, and Bernanke has already received the prize. Gertler is also in B049, so there is some overlap.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from 1989 to 1997 and has been thoroughly validated by later macro-finance work. The timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 banking-crisis prize.
Whether Gertler or Gilchrist should be included alongside Kiyotaki and Moore.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based approach to technology and labour demand, together with the China-shock evidence, reshaped understanding of wage polarisation and the distributional effects of trade and automation. The empirical and policy influence is very high.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both strands. Hanson is central to the trade-shock evidence, and Katz to skill-biased change and the race between education and technology. Dorn is a key coauthor but more junior.
assessment.maturity: The work is 10 to 25 years old. The China-shock results are well replicated but their interpretation is still debated, and the AI-era extensions are unsettled.
uncertainties: Some debate over the interpretation and persistence of the China-shock effects.
Katz's overlap with the mobility candidacy (B017).
Whether the field is mature enough compared with older candidacies.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm trade models with selection into exporting explain intra-industry reallocation and the gains from trade, and brought firm-level data to the centre of international economics. The framework is widely used. It is also close to my own interests in firm-level pricing and export behaviour, so I note a possible bias toward it.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) and related work extend it, and Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are also relevant but are not credited in this entry. Redding is a plausible contributor but less central to the original insight.
assessment.maturity: The work is over 20 years old and has been confirmed through extensive firm-level evidence. The framework's quantitative role is now partly shared with the Ricardian approaches in B031.
uncertainties: Omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum from the credited list.
Helpman's overlap with B021.
Whether trade is likely to be rewarded again soon after 2008.
